wording: Greek (descriptive): ancient Greek theories of soul (psuchê) differ widely — Plato, Aristotle, Epicurus and the Stoics give the main accounts — and for some thinkers the ensouled includes plants.
Greek (descriptive): Aristotle defines soul as the first actuality of a natural body having life potentially — soul as form of the living body.
Greek (descriptive): Epicurus held the soul to be atomic and dispersed at death; the Stoics treated soul as pneuma, a breath-like material compound, with the commanding faculty located at the heart.

wording: Hebrew Bible (descriptive): Genesis 2:7 says God formed the human from the soil and blew into his nostrils the breath of life, and the human became a 'living being' (Hebrew nefesh ḥayyah).
counterevidence_limits: One verse only; the wider semantic range of nefesh across the Hebrew Bible was not surveyed.

wording: Christian (descriptive): Aquinas defines the soul as the first principle of life and argues that the intellectual principle is incorporeal and subsistent.
locator: Summa Theologiae I q.75 aa.1–2 ('I answer that')
counterevidence_limits: One medieval theologian; Christian views vary.
verification_phrases: U40|first principle of life || U40|incorporeal and subsistent

wording: Islamic (descriptive): Qur'an 17:85 (Saheeh International) answers a question about the rūḥ: 'The soul is of the affair of my Lord. And mankind have not been given of knowledge except a little'; 15:29 speaks of God breathing into the human of His [created] soul.
verification_phrases: U41|affair of my Lord || U50|breathed into him

wording: Islamic philosophy (descriptive): Avicenna's 'floating man' thought experiment and Averroes' doctrine of the unity of the intellect are notable contributions in the dualist tradition.

Hindu (descriptive): Bhagavad Gita 2.20 (Prabhupada translation) says the soul is unborn and eternal and is not slain when the body is slain; Advaita Vedānta identifies the individual self (ātman) with Brahman.
counterevidence_limits: Sectarian translation (ISKCON); other Hindu schools differ.
verification_phrases: U43|not slain when the body is slain

wording: Buddhist (descriptive): Indian Buddhist philosophy counts the lack of an abiding self (anātman) among the three marks of existence.
Chinese (descriptive): early Chinese texts speak of hun and po souls and of qi; xin ('heart-mind') originated as a picture of the heart and is credited with thinking, understanding and feeling.
African (descriptive): in African ethics as presented by Gyekye, character and moral personhood are central and morality is social rather than individualistic.
counterevidence_limits: One author's synthesis across many cultures; generalization risk.

wording: Indigenous (descriptive): animist traditions common to many Indigenous cultures treat features of the environment (trees, rivers, animals) as non-human persons and relatives; social-relational readings do not require a doctrine of interior souls.
counterevidence_limits: Outsider encyclopaedia synthesis; Indigenous traditions are plural and self-described differently.

wording: Identity: whether the person is a soul, an organism, or a psychologically continuous subject is contested (psychological-continuity views vs animalism vs soul views).
Moral character: virtue ethics, one of three major approaches in normative ethics, emphasizes the virtues or moral character (vs duties or consequences).
Purpose: accounts of life's meaning divide into supernaturalist (God- or soul-centred), naturalist and nihilist views; none is established.
Independence from body: substance dualism, hylomorphic dualism and physicalism compete; dualism faces the interaction problem and causal-closure objections.
